claim: Worldwide, an estimated 240 million people suffer from chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV).
source: Worldwide, an estimated 240 million people suffer from chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV); infection is most often acquired in early childhood.
evidence: This is a factual statement about HBV prevalence that is supported by citation to Gish et al., 2015 in the manuscript.

claim: HBV infection is most often acquired in early childhood.
source: Worldwide, an estimated 240 million people suffer from chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV); infection is most often acquired in early childhood.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Gish et al., 2015.

claim: Chronic HBV can lead to liver disease including liver failure, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma.
source: Over time, chronic HBV can lead to liver disease including liver failure, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, contributing to more than 700,000 deaths each year (Gish et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gish et al., 2015.

claim: Chronic HBV contributes to more than 700,000 deaths each year.
source: Over time, chronic HBV can lead to liver disease including liver failure, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma, contributing to more than 700,000 deaths each year (Gish et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gish et al., 2015.

claim: A vaccine directed against surface protein is preventative but not therapeutic for HBV.
source: A vaccine directed against surface protein is preventative but not therapeutic.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HBV vaccines.

claim: Entry inhibitors prevent new infection but are unlikely to affect maintenance of a chronic infection.
source: Entry inhibitors prevent new infection but are unlikely to affect maintenance of a chronic infection (Volz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Volz et al., 2013.

claim: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors directed against the viral polymerase suppress viremia and improve liver health.
source: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors directed against the viral polymerase suppress viremia and improve liver health, but even after years of treatment are rarely curative (Gish et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gish et al., 2007 and Shi et al., 2015.

claim: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors are rarely curative even after years of treatment.
source: Reverse transcriptase inhibitors directed against the viral polymerase suppress viremia and improve liver health, but even after years of treatment are rarely curative (Gish et al., 2007; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gish et al., 2007 and Shi et al., 2015.

claim: Interferon α and derivatives can stimulate HBV clearance in a small subset of patients.
source: Interferon α and derivatives can stimulate HBV clearance in a small subset of patients (Gish et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gish et al., 2015.

claim: The viral core protein (Cp) has become an important target for developing direct-acting antivirals (DAAs).
source: The viral core protein (Cp) has become an important target for developing direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) (Zlotnick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zlotnick et al., 2015.

claim: HBV Cp is present at virtually every step of the virus lifecycle in an infected cell.
source: The HBV Cp is present at virtually every step of the virus lifecycle in an infected cell (Zlotnick et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zlotnick et al., 2015.

claim: In the nucleus, Cp is associated with viral nucleic acid.
source: In the nucleus, Cp is associated with viral nucleic acid (Bock et al., 2001; Li et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bock et al., 2001 and Li et al., 2010.

claim: In cytoplasm, Cp assembly packages viral polymerase complexed with an RNA copy of the viral genome.
source: In cytoplasm, Cp assembly packages viral polymerase complexed with an RNA copy of the viral genome and has an active role in reverse transcription of the relaxed circular mature genome (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claim: Cp has an active role in reverse transcription of the relaxed circular mature genome.
source: In cytoplasm, Cp assembly packages viral polymerase complexed with an RNA copy of the viral genome and has an active role in reverse transcription of the relaxed circular mature genome (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claim: Cp has signals that direct core intracellular trafficking and secretion of enveloped cores.
source: Cp also has signals that direct core intracellular trafficking and secretion of enveloped cores (Kann et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kann et al., 2007.

claim: When transported to the nucleus, the core disassembles to release its contents.
source: When transported to the nucleus, for new infection and to maintain infection, the core disassembles to release its contents.
evidence: This is established knowledge about HBV core protein function.

claim: Approximately 90% of the capsids from enveloped particles are empty and the rest contain the viral genome.
source: Curiously, approximately 90% of the capsids from enveloped particles are empty and the rest contain the viral genome (Ning et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ning et al., 2011.

claim: Assembly can be nucleated by a polymerase-viral RNA complex for virions or spontaneously by Cp.
source: This leads to the hypothesis that assembly can be nucleated by a polymerase-viral RNA complex for virions or spontaneously by Cp.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis based on the observation about empty and full capsids.

claim: The oligomeric nature of Cp function makes it a particularly attractive antiviral target because even when DAA-resistant mutants arise, residual wildtype protein co-assembled into a complex retains DAA sensitivity.
source: The oligomeric nature of Cp function makes it a particularly attractive antiviral target because even when DAA-resistant mutants arise, residual wildtype protein co-assembled into a complex retains DAA sensitivity (Tanner et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tanner et al., 2014.

claim: The HBV Cp is a 183-residue, homodimeric protein.
source: The HBV Cp is a 183-residue, homodimeric protein (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The first 149 residues of Cp form the assembly domain.
source: The first 149 residues form the assembly domain.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HBV core protein.

claim: Each monomer contributes two helices to a four-helix bundle that forms the intradimer interface.
source: Each monomer contributes two helices to a four-helix bundle that forms the intradimer interface (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: The final 34 residues of the full length Cp form the disordered nucleic acid-binding C-terminal domain.
source: The final 34 residues of the full length Cp form the disordered nucleic acid-binding C-terminal domain.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HBV core protein.

claim: The C-terminal domain is optional for capsid assembly but required for nucleic acid packaging.
source: This domain is optional for capsid assembly but required for nucleic acid packaging; this region also carries putative nuclear localization and nuclear export signals (Li et al., 2010; Kann et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2010 and Kann et al., 2007.

claim: The C-terminal domain carries putative nuclear localization and nuclear export signals.
source: This domain is optional for capsid assembly but required for nucleic acid packaging; this region also carries putative nuclear localization and nuclear export signals (Li et al., 2010; Kann et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2010 and Kann et al., 2007.

claim: Cp assembles into icosahedral 90-dimer T = 3 capsids and 120-dimer T = 4 capsids.
source: Cp assembles into icosahedral 90-dimer T = 3 capsids and 120-dimer T = 4 capsids.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HBV capsid assembly.

claim: In capsids, dimers are arranged in a pattern of fivefold vertices and quasi-sixfold vertices.
source: In capsids, dimers are arranged in a pattern of fivefold vertices and quasi-sixfold vertices.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about icosahedral capsids.

claim: A T = 3 capsid is comprised of 60 AB dimers and 30 CC dimers (with true twofold symmetry).
source: Thus, owing to quasi-equivalence, a T = 3 capsid is comprised of 60 AB dimers and 30 CC dimers (with true twofold symmetry) and a T = 4 capsid is comprised of 60 AB and 60 CD dimers.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HBV capsid composition.

claim: A T = 4 capsid is comprised of 60 AB and 60 CD dimers.
source: Thus, owing to quasi-equivalence, a T = 3 capsid is comprised of 60 AB dimers and 30 CC dimers (with true twofold symmetry) and a T = 4 capsid is comprised of 60 AB and 60 CD dimers.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about HBV capsid composition.

claim: In vitro assembly of the assembly domain or full-length Cp yields about 90% T = 4 capsids.
source: In vitro assembly of the assembly domain or full-length Cp yields about 90% T = 4 capsids; a similar ratio is observed in vivo (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016; Stannard and Hodgkiss, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016 and Stannard and Hodgkiss, 1979.

claim: A similar ratio of T = 4 to T = 3 capsids is observed in vivo.
source: In vitro assembly of the assembly domain or full-length Cp yields about 90% T = 4 capsids; a similar ratio is observed in vivo (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016; Stannard and Hodgkiss, 1979).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016 and Stannard and Hodgkiss, 1979.

claim: Assembly is hypothesized to be initiated by a conformational transition of Cp to an active state.
source: It is hypothesized that assembly is initiated by a conformational transition of Cp to an active state, suggesting a basis for regulated assembly in vivo (Packianathan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Packianathan et al., 2010.

claim: The net association energy of Cp dimers is weak.
source: The net association energy is weak, but since each of the many Cp dimers forming a capsid are tetravalent, the result is a globally stable structure (Zlotnick, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zlotnick, 2003.

claim: Each of the many Cp dimers forming a capsid are tetravalent, resulting in a globally stable structure.
source: The net association energy is weak, but since each of the many Cp dimers forming a capsid are tetravalent, the result is a globally stable structure (Zlotnick, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Zlotnick, 2003.

claim: In vitro assembly of HBV Cp is sensitive to ions and temperature.
source: In vitro assembly of HBV Cp is sensitive to ions and temperature, supporting the hypothesis that assembly can be allosterically regulated (Stray et al., 2004; Ceres et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stray et al., 2004 and Ceres et al., 2004.

claim: There is a close relationship between the familiar phenomenon of allostery and the structural principle of tensegrity in virus capsids.
source: Furthermore, there is a close relationship between the familiar phenomenon of allostery and the structural principle of tensegrity in virus capsids (Domitrovic et al., 2013a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Domitrovic et al., 2013a.

claim: Putative Cp allosteric effectors (e.g. heteraryldihydropyrmidines or HAPs) have been discovered that have antiviral effect.
source: Putative Cp allosteric effectors (e.g. heteraryldihydropyrmidines or HAPs) have been discovered that have antiviral effect (Deres et al., 2003; Stray et al., 2005; Stray and Zlotnick, 2006a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Deres et al., 2003, Stray et al., 2005, and Stray and Zlotnick, 2006a.

claim: HAPs ostensibly act by inducing an assembly-active state and by stabilizing Cp-Cp interactions by filling a pocket at the interdimer interface between dimers of the quasi-sixfold.
source: These small molecules ostensibly act by inducing an assembly-active state and by stabilizing Cp-Cp interactions by filling a pocket at the interdimer interface between dimers of the quasi-sixfold (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016; Bourne et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016 and Bourne et al., 2006.

claim: The well-characterized mechanism for CpAM action is to over-initiate assembly, forming empty capsids and large aberrant structures.
source: The well-characterized mechanism for CpAM action is to over-initiate assembly, forming empty capsids and large aberrant structures.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CpAM mechanism of action.

claim: Both empty capsids and large aberrant structures act to sequester Cp from its biological functions.
source: Both products act to sequester Cp from its biological functions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mechanism of CpAM action.

claim: HAP-TAMRA induced Cp assembly.
source: HAP-TAMRA induced Cp assembly and also bound pre-assembled capsids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: HAP-TAMRA bound pre-assembled capsids.
source: HAP-TAMRA induced Cp assembly and also bound pre-assembled capsids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c,d.

claim: Kinetic and spectroscopic studies imply that HAP-binding sites are usually not available but are bound cooperatively.
source: Kinetic and spectroscopic studies imply that HAP-binding sites are usually not available but are bound cooperatively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: HAP-TAMRA asymmetrically deformed capsids, creating a heterogeneous array of sharp angles, flat regions, and outright breaks.
source: Using cryo-EM, we observed that HAP-TAMRA asymmetrically deformed capsids, creating a heterogeneous array of sharp angles, flat regions, and outright breaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4.

claim: A disulfide crosslink rescued particle symmetry.
source: To achieve high resolution reconstruction (<4 Å), we introduced a disulfide crosslink that rescued particle symmetry.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing Cp149 and Cp150 in Figure 4.

claim: HAP-TAMRA caused quasi-sixfold vertices to become flatter and fivefold more angular.
source: We deduced that HAP-TAMRA caused quasi-sixfold vertices to become flatter and fivefold more angular.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figures 9 and 10.

claim: The flattening of quasi-sixfold vertices led to asymmetric faceting.
source: This transition led to asymmetric faceting.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural changes observed.

claim: That a disordered crosslink could rescue symmetry implies that capsids have tensegrity properties.
source: That a disordered crosslink could rescue symmetry implies that capsids have tensegrity properties.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental observation with Cp150.

claim: Capsid distortion and disruption is a new mechanism by which molecules like the HAPs can block HBV infection.
source: Capsid distortion and disruption is a new mechanism by which molecules like the HAPs can block HBV infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental findings in this study.

claim: HAP-TAMRA's HAP13 core was extended with a three-carbon linker appended with a tetramethylrhodamine (TAMRA) dye.
source: HAP-TAMRA's HAP13 core (Bourne et al., 2008) was extended with a three-carbon linker appended with a tetramethylrhodamine (TAMRA) dye.
evidence: This is a description of the synthesis of HAP-TAMRA.

claim: The HAP13 core used in HAP-TAMRA synthesis was a racemic mixture.
source: As the HAP13 core used in this synthesis was a racemic mixture, only half the compound is expected to be active (Deres et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about the chemical composition of the synthesized compound.

claim: Only half of the HAP-TAMRA compound is expected to be active.
source: As the HAP13 core used in this synthesis was a racemic mixture, only half the compound is expected to be active (Deres et al., 2003).
evidence: This is based on the racemic nature of the synthesis and citation to Deres et al., 2003.

claim: HAP-TAMRA in the presence of purified core protein produced large aberrant products that are characteristic of HAP-induced assembly.
source: We observed that assembly reactions of purified core protein in the presence of HAP-TAMRA produced large aberrant products that are characteristic of HAP-induced assembly (Figure 2b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Assembly reactions without CpAMs led to particles morphologically consistent with an icosahedral shell.
source: For reference, assembly reactions without CpAMs (Figure 2b) led to particles morphologically consistent with an icosahedral shell.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: HAP-TAMRA co-eluted with capsid in size exclusion chromatography.
source: Capsids co-eluted with bound HAP-TAMRA in the capsid fraction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Free HAP-TAMRA eluted at the end of the column volume.
source: Free HAP-TAMRA eluted at the end of the column volume, as expected for a small molecule.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: TAMRA absorbance spectra associated with the capsid and free probe were distinctly different.
source: TAMRA absorbance spectra associated with the capsid and free probe were distinctly different.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c inset.

claim: The free probe exhibited the familiar absorbance profile of TAMRA, with a major peak near 555 nm, and a shoulder at 520 nm.
source: The free probe exhibited the familiar absorbance profile of TAMRA, with a major peak near 555 nm, and a shoulder at 520 nm.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c inset.

claim: The absorbance spectrum for capsid-bound HAP-TAMRA was shifted, with a major peak near 520 nm and a shoulder around 550 nm.
source: The absorbance spectrum for capsid-bound HAP-TAMRA was shifted, with a major peak near 520 nm and a shoulder around 550 nm that resembled examples of spectra from π-stacked TAMRA complexes (Adachi et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c inset and citation to Adachi et al., 2014.

claim: The signal associated with capsid peaked at about one HAP-TAMRA per dimer.
source: For both the absorbance at 520 nm and the 520/555 ratio, the signal associated with capsid peaked at about one HAP-TAMRA per dimer.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: HAP-TAMRA binds capsid with high affinity compared to the 8 µM Cp dimer used in these experiments.
source: These data also suggest that HAP-TAMRA binds capsid with high affinity compared to the 8 µM Cp dimer used in these experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the binding data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Binding of HAP-TAMRA to capsids reached half-saturation in approximately 10 min at all concentrations tested.
source: Using 2.5 to 40 µM HAP-TAMRA, we observed that binding was surprisingly slow, reaching half-saturation in approximately 10 min at all concentrations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The rate of binding under these conditions was independent of HAP-TAMRA concentration.
source: When the different kinetic trajectories were normalized to the same maximum and minimum values, zero and one, it was evident that they were identical (Figure 3c), indicating that the rate of binding under these conditions was independent of HAP-TAMRA concentration.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The average for the fast half-life of HAP-TAMRA binding was 0.6 ± 0.1 min.
source: The average for the fast half-life was 0.6 ± 0.1 min and for the slow half-life was 7.1 ± 1.4 min (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The average for the slow half-life of HAP-TAMRA binding was 7.1 ± 1.4 min.
source: The average for the fast half-life was 0.6 ± 0.1 min and for the slow half-life was 7.1 ± 1.4 min (Figure 3b).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The primary barrier for HAP binding is a conformational transition at the site of the binding pocket.
source: This HAP-TAMRA concentration independence and the slow binding rate strongly suggest that the primary barrier for HAP binding is a conformational transition at the site of the binding pocket.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: The change in absorbance increased linearly until capsids were saturated at one HAP-TAMRA per dimer.
source: We observed that the change in absorbance increased linearly until capsids were saturated at one HAP-TAMRA per dimer (Figure 2d).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: The change in extinction coefficient for bound HAP-TAMRA was 11200 ± 4% M−1.
source: The change in absorbance per bound HAP-TAMRA was also evaluated (i.e. the change in extinction coefficient) and found to be 11200 ± 4% M−1 (Figure 3e).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: There is the same degree of TAMRA–TAMRA interaction in saturated capsids and in capsids where there was on average only one HAP-TAMRA per capsid.
source: This result indicates that there is the same degree of TAMRA–TAMRA interaction in saturated capsids and in capsids where there was on average only one HAP-TAMRA per capsid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the constant extinction coefficient shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The change in absorbance spectrum suggested TAMRA-TAMRA interaction that would be expected to cause static quenching.
source: The change in absorbance spectrum suggested TAMRA-TAMRA interaction that would be expected to cause static quenching; this prediction was confirmed in Figure 3f where the residual fluorescence is largely due to unbound probe.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claim: In both raw micrographs and 2D class averages, the heterogeneity of particle shapes with bound HAP was evident.
source: However, in both raw micrographs and 2D class averages, the heterogeneity of particle shapes with bound HAP was evident (Figure 4a,c): many particles had sharp corners, facets, and irregular outlines.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4a,c.

claim: Many particles with bound HAP-TAMRA had sharp corners, facets, and irregular outlines.
source: However, in both raw micrographs and 2D class averages, the heterogeneity of particle shapes with bound HAP was evident (Figure 4a,c): many particles had sharp corners, facets, and irregular outlines.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4a,c.

claim: Apo-capsids had a round cross section with obvious spikes and distinct internal features.
source: Apo-capsids (Figure 4b) had a round cross section with obvious spikes and distinct internal features.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Capsids with HAP-TAMRA had a broad distribution of asymmetric shapes with ellipsoidal character and distinct faceting.
source: The capsids with HAP-TAMRA had a broad distribution of asymmetric shapes with ellipsoidal character and distinct faceting.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Cp150 is a variant of Cp149 with an engineered disulfide bond linking the disordered C-terminal tails when in capsid form.
source: Therefore, we examined Cp150 capsids; Cp150 is a variant of Cp149 with an engineered disulfide bond linking the disordered C-terminal tails when in capsid form (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2017.

claim: The 2D class averages of Cp150 capsids incubated with HAP-TAMRA showed regular and approximately spherical particles.
source: The 2D class averages of Cp150 capsids incubated with HAP-TAMRA (Figure 4c) showed regular and approximately spherical particles; suitable for further detailed structural analysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: T = 4 Cp150-HAP-TAMRA capsids were reconstructed to 4.0 Å resolution.
source: To examine HAP-bound capsids, we reconstructed T = 4 and T = 3 Cp150-HAP-TAMRA capsids to 4.0 Å and 3.7 Å resolution, respectively, from a single dataset (Figures 5 and 6; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction data shown in Figures 5, 6 and Table 1.

claim: T = 3 Cp150-HAP-TAMRA capsids were reconstructed to 3.7 Å resolution.
source: To examine HAP-bound capsids, we reconstructed T = 4 and T = 3 Cp150-HAP-TAMRA capsids to 4.0 Å and 3.7 Å resolution, respectively, from a single dataset (Figures 5 and 6; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by cryo-EM reconstruction data shown in Figures 5, 6 and Table 1.

claim: The T = 4 capsids were slightly larger than crystallographic structures.
source: The T = 4 capsids were slightly larger than crystallographic structures, though each crystal structure has shown unique features (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous crystallographic structures with citation.

claim: In T = 4 capsids, quasi-sixfold hexamers have four HAP-TAMRA molecules.
source: In T = 4 capsids, quasi-sixfold hexamers have four HAP-TAMRA molecules, while the T = 3 quasi-sixfold hexamers accommodate three HAP-TAMRA molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: T = 3 quasi-sixfold hexamers accommodate three HAP-TAMRA molecules.
source: In T = 4 capsids, quasi-sixfold hexamers have four HAP-TAMRA molecules, while the T = 3 quasi-sixfold hexamers accommodate three HAP-TAMRA molecules.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The HAP13 portion of the probe is nestled in the pocket between two adjacent dimers with the linker extending from the pocket, positioning the TAMRA near the center of the quasi-sixfold pore.
source: The HAP13 portion of the probe is nestled in the pocket between two adjacent dimers with the linker extending from the pocket, positioning the TAMRA near the center of the quasi-sixfold pore.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5 and Figure 7.

claim: In the T = 4 quasi-sixfold, the HAPs are in B, C, B', and C' pockets, which are respectively capped by C, D, C' and D' subunits.
source: In the T = 4 quasi-sixfold, the HAPs are in B, C, B', and C' pockets, which are respectively capped by C, D, C' and D' subunits (Figure 5b).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: In the T = 3 particles, HAPs are in B pockets capped by C subunits.
source: In the T = 3 particles, HAPs are in B pockets capped by C subunits (Figure 5d).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: No small molecule density was observed at the corresponding A (fivefold) and D sites.
source: No small molecule density was observed at the corresponding A (fivefold) and D sites, which are occluded by A and B subunits, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The pocket of the T = 3 C subunit is occluded by the neighboring B subunit, resembling the interaction of the T = 4 D subunit with its neighboring B subunit.
source: The pocket of the T = 3 C subunit is occluded by the neighboring B subunit, resembling the interaction of the T = 4 D subunit with its neighboring B subunit.
evidence: This is a structural comparison based on the cryo-EM data.

claim: The local environment of the HAP-TAMRA in the HAP pocket was remarkably similar between T = 3 and T = 4 capsids.
source: Despite the quaternary differences between T = 3 and T = 4 capsids, the local environment of the HAP-TAMRA in the HAP pocket was remarkably similar (Figure 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The HAP13 had extremely well-ordered density in the pocket.
source: The HAP13 had extremely well-ordered density in the pocket as do most protein side chains in the region (visualized in Figure 7e at a contour of 3.6 σ, where σ is the number of standard deviations from the mean).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7e.

claim: The quality of HAP-TAMRA density gradually decays in the TAMRA region.
source: The quality of HAP-TAMRA density gradually decays in the TAMRA region, which is visible as a loss of density in Figure 7, and was also seen as a decay in local resolution in Figure 8.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: The loss of density in the TAMRA region is consistent with fewer positional constraints in the exposed TAMRA moiety, and higher molecular motion.
source: This observation is consistent with fewer positional constraints in the exposed TAMRA moiety, and higher molecular motion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: For the T = 4 C subunit, the TAMRA density is only contiguous at 2.6 σ.
source: In particular, the T = 4 C subunit the TAMRA density is only contiguous at 2.6 σ.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Linker density clearly points towards a planar mass that is parallel to and 'stacked' on the TAMRA from the B' subunit.
source: However, linker density clearly points towards a planar mass that is parallel to and 'stacked' on the TAMRA from the B' subunit.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: 80–90% of the capsids have T = 4 symmetry.
source: However, as 80–90% of the capsids have T = 4 symmetry, we suggest that these TAMRA-TAMRA interactions are the cause of the observed change in the optical signal (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is established knowledge about HBV capsid composition.

claim: TAMRA-TAMRA interactions in T = 4 capsids are the cause of the observed change in the optical signal.
source: However, as 80–90% of the capsids have T = 4 symmetry, we suggest that these TAMRA-TAMRA interactions are the cause of the observed change in the optical signal (Figure 2c,d).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural and spectroscopic data.

claim: Local similarities in protein structure do not translate to similarities one or two dimers away when comparing T = 3 to T = 4, and T = 4 CpAM-bound to T = 4 apo structures.
source: When comparing T = 3 to T = 4, and T = 4 CpAM-bound to T = 4 apo structures, we found that local similarities in protein structure do not translate to similarities one or two dimers away.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural comparisons.

claim: Long range differences in quaternary structure were apparent when overlaying entire hexamers.
source: Long range differences in quaternary structure were apparent when overlaying entire hexamers, for example overlaying T = 3 and T = 4 quasi-sixfold hexamers based on one set of AB dimers (Figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data shown in Figure 9.

claim: The dramatic effect arises because the small angular differences are amplified by distance.
source: The dramatic effect arises because the small angular differences are amplified by distance.
evidence: This is an explanation for the observed structural differences.

claim: The Y132A mutation disrupts normal interdimer interaction allowing crystal contacts that form hexagonal layers reminiscent of but distinct from subunit interactions in capsids.
source: The Y132A mutation disrupts normal interdimer interaction allowing crystal contacts that form hexagonal layers reminiscent of but distinct from subunit interactions in capsids.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Y132A mutant with citations.

claim: CpAM-induced quaternary differences between HBV capsids do not appear arise from changes in the binding to the HAP pocket.
source: Such CpAM-induced quaternary differences between HBV capsids do not appear arise from changes in the binding to the HAP pocket.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis.

claim: CpAM-induced quaternary differences arise from the way the capping subunit overlays the pocket and how these differences propagate across a capsid.
source: Rather, they arise from the way the capping subunit overlays the pocket and how these differences propagate across a capsid.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on structural analysis.

claim: The HAP-bound particle has expanded, particularly at the fivefold.
source: It is immediately clear that the HAP-bound particle has expanded, particularly at the fivefold (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The cryo-EM reconstruction shows a greater expansion than seen in crystallographic structures of other CpAM-capsid complexes.
source: The cryo-EM reconstruction shows a greater expansion than seen in crystallographic structures of other CpAM-capsid complexes (Bourne et al., 2006; Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016; Katen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous crystallographic structures with citations.

claim: In comparison to the apo capsid, the displacement maximum is almost 6 Å around the 5-fold axis.
source: In comparison to the apo capsid, the displacement maximum is almost 6 Å around the 5-fold axis, and the displacement minimum is 1.7 Å around the 3-fold axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The displacement minimum is 1.7 Å around the 3-fold axis.
source: In comparison to the apo capsid, the displacement maximum is almost 6 Å around the 5-fold axis, and the displacement minimum is 1.7 Å around the 3-fold axis.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural comparison data shown in Figure 10.

claim: The two-dimer asymmetric unit is rotated along the long axis of the CD dimer, near the 3-fold, leading the AB dimer to pivot upward, raising at the 5-fold.
source: The two-dimer asymmetric unit is rotated along the long axis of the CD dimer, near the 3-fold, leading the AB dimer to pivot upward, raising at the 5-fold.
evidence: This is a description of the structural changes observed.

claim: The basis of this quaternary change is a flattening of the quasi-sixfold hexamers.
source: We suggest that the basis of this quaternary change is a flattening of the quasi-sixfold hexamers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the structural data.

claim: Flattening quasi-sixfold and concomitantly making the 5-fold vertices protrude is likely a subdued version of what we observed for Cp149.
source: Flattening quasi-sixfold and concomitantly making the 5-fold vertices protrude is likely a subdued version of what we observed for Cp149 (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference connecting the Cp150 and Cp149 observations.

claim: The structural variation that leads to faceting of T = 4 capsids can be observed by examining the cryo-EM local resolution maps.
source: An important observation is that the structural variation that leads to faceting of T = 4 capsids can also be observed by examining the cryo-EM local resolution maps (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The local resolution is systematically better around the 2-fold symmetry axis, and worse around the 5-fold.
source: The local resolution is systematically better around the 2-fold symmetry axis, and worse around the 5-fold.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The result suggests a greater positional variation of A subunits, equivalent to a crystallographic B factor.
source: This result suggests a greater positional variation of A subunits, equivalent to a crystallographic B factor.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the local resolution data.

claim: In both AB and CD dimers, the highest resolution is observed in the core of the protein, the chassis subdomain.
source: In both AB and CD dimers, the highest resolution is observed in the core of the protein, the chassis subdomain (Packianathan et al., 2010), and the lowest resolution, falling to about 5 Å, is at the spike tips.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The lowest resolution, falling to about 5 Å, is at the spike tips.
source: In both AB and CD dimers, the highest resolution is observed in the core of the protein, the chassis subdomain (Packianathan et al., 2010), and the lowest resolution, falling to about 5 Å, is at the spike tips.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Protein–protein interactions around the quasi-sixfold were extremely well-ordered.
source: Protein–protein interactions around the quasi-sixfold were extremely well-ordered as were the HAP moieties of HAP-TAMRA, about 3.6 Å in the overall 4 Å resolution T = 4 structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The HAP moieties of HAP-TAMRA were extremely well-ordered, about 3.6 Å in the overall 4 Å resolution T = 4 structure.
source: Protein–protein interactions around the quasi-sixfold were extremely well-ordered as were the HAP moieties of HAP-TAMRA, about 3.6 Å in the overall 4 Å resolution T = 4 structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The resolution of the TAMRA density was poorer, about 5 Å.
source: The resolution of the TAMRA density was poorer, about 5 Å.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural data.

claim: The Cp149 +HAP TAMRA reconstruction could only reach 22 Å resolution.
source: The Cp149 +HAP TAMRA reconstruction could only reach 22 Å resolution, which is a likely outcome from icosahedral averaging a wide array of structural states.
evidence: This claim is supported by reconstruction data shown in Figure 11.

claim: The striking feature of the Cp149 +HAP TAMRA reconstruction is the absence of density at the fivefold.
source: The striking feature of the reconstruction is the absence of density at the fivefold.
evidence: This claim is supported by reconstruction data shown in Figure 11a.

claim: The absence of density at the fivefold may arise because the A subunits are extremely mobile or that the individual A subunits are relatively static but in a variety of positions.
source: This may arise because the A subunits are extremely mobile or, more likely, that the individual A subunits are relatively static but in a variety of positions.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the missing density.

claim: The A subunits are the favored site of capsid failure.
source: This result suggests that the A subunits are the favored site of capsid failure.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: CpAMs can distort capsid shape.
source: CpAMs, exemplified here by HAP-TAMRA, can distort capsid shape.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: HAP-TAMRA with crosslinked Cp150 dimers yielded capsids that retained icosahedral symmetry and were suitable for relatively high-resolution reconstruction.
source: HAP-TAMRA with crosslinked Cp150 dimers yielded capsids that retained icosahedral symmetry and were suitable for relatively high-resolution reconstruction.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4-8.

claim: HAP-TAMRA with the uncrosslinked capsids of Cp149 led to asymmetric faceting, severe distortions, and broken capsids.
source: HAP-TAMRA with the uncrosslinked capsids of Cp149 led to asymmetric faceting, severe distortions, and broken capsids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Defects in the capsid structure due to CpAMs may alter exposure of signals for cellular trafficking.
source: Defects in the capsid structure due to CpAMs may alter exposure of signals for cellular trafficking (Kann et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2016) or dysregulate capsid dissociation (Rabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about the biological consequences with citations.

claim: Defects in the capsid structure due to CpAMs may dysregulate capsid dissociation.
source: Defects in the capsid structure due to CpAMs may alter exposure of signals for cellular trafficking (Kann et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2016) or dysregulate capsid dissociation (Rabe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is speculation about the biological consequences with citation.

claim: Core protein and capsid play active roles in reverse transcription which would be expected to be compromised in a deformed capsid.
source: Core protein and capsid play active roles in reverse transcription which we would expect to also be compromised in a deformed capsid (Nassal, 2008; Hu and Seeger, 2015; Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about the biological consequences with citations.

claim: Core protein mutations that fill the HAP site lead to defects in both RNA packaging and transcription of the DNA plus-sense strand.
source: Core protein mutations that fill the HAP site lead to defects in both RNA packaging and transcription of the DNA plus-sense strand suggesting that CpAMs can have similar action (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Tan et al., 2015.

claim: CpAMs can have similar action to mutations that fill the HAP site.
source: Core protein mutations that fill the HAP site lead to defects in both RNA packaging and transcription of the DNA plus-sense strand suggesting that CpAMs can have similar action (Tan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the mutational data.

claim: The T = 4 Cp150+HAP TAMRA cryo-EM structure has a larger diameter than crystallographic structures of the apo capsid and CpAM-bound capsids.
source: The T = 4 Cp150+HAP TAMRA cryo-EM structure has a larger diameter than crystallographic structures of the apo capsid (Wynne et al., 1999a) and CpAM-bound capsids (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous crystallographic structures with citations.

claim: The HAP pockets show little structural difference in quasi-equivalent sites in capsids or in crystal structures of the assembly-incompetent mutant Y132A.
source: The HAP pockets show little structural difference in quasi-equivalent sites in capsids or in crystal structures of the assembly-incompetent mutant Y132A (Packianathan et al., 2010; Zhou et al., 2017; Klumpp et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous crystallographic structures with citations.

claim: CpAM is affecting structure primarily by modulating the protein-protein interactions of the capping subunit.
source: This indicates that CpAM is affecting structure primarily by modulating the protein-protein interactions of the capping subunit.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: CpAMs can subtly modify the tertiary and quaternary structure of an individual dimer.
source: In addition, CpAMs can subtly modify the tertiary and quaternary structure of an individual dimer (Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: In broad terms, CpAMs flatten sixfold.
source: In broad terms, CpAMs flatten sixfold; during assembly this can result in non-capsid structures with extended regions of hexagonal sheet (Stray et al., 2005). or cylinders with a hexagonal repeat (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stray et al., 2005 and Liu et al., 2017.

claim: During assembly, CpAMs can result in non-capsid structures with extended regions of hexagonal sheet.
source: In broad terms, CpAMs flatten sixfold; during assembly this can result in non-capsid structures with extended regions of hexagonal sheet (Stray et al., 2005). or cylinders with a hexagonal repeat (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Stray et al., 2005.

claim: During assembly, CpAMs can result in cylinders with a hexagonal repeat.
source: In broad terms, CpAMs flatten sixfold; during assembly this can result in non-capsid structures with extended regions of hexagonal sheet (Stray et al., 2005). or cylinders with a hexagonal repeat (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017.

claim: The flattening of quasi-sixfold, observed in molecular detail in the crosslinked Cp150 capsid, is also evident in uncrosslinked Cp149 capsids as flat regions and sharp angles.
source: The flattening of quasi-sixfold, observed in molecular detail in the crosslinked Cp150 capsid, is also evident in uncrosslinked Cp149 capsids as flat regions and sharp angles.
evidence: This is a conclusion connecting observations from Cp150 and Cp149.

claim: The sharp angles are likely to arise at fivefold.
source: The sharp angles are likely to arise at fivefold.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Phage P22 is assembled as a rounded procapsids that matures to have flattened sixfold and sharply angled fivefold.
source: This is analogous to phage P22 which is assembled as a rounded procapsids that matures to have flattened sixfold and sharply angled fivefold (Teschke and Parent, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Teschke and Parent, 2010.

claim: In the 22 Å resolution image reconstruction, the absence of density at fivefold could be due to highly dynamic A subunits, or to relatively static structures where the A subunits have multiple orientations.
source: In the 22 Å resolution image reconstruction (Figure 10c), the absence of density at fivefold could be due to highly dynamic A subunits, or to relatively static structures where the A subunits have multiple orientations.
evidence: This is speculation about the cause of the missing density.

claim: Retaining the flattened region must be energetically more favored than maintaining the global capsid structure for a flattened quasi-sixfold to disrupt a complete capsid.
source: For a flattened quasi-sixfold to disrupt a complete capsid, retaining the flattened region must be energetically more favored than maintaining the global capsid structure.
evidence: This is an inference about the energetics of the system.

claim: CpAMs are known to strengthen protein-protein interaction energy.
source: CpAMs are known to strengthen protein-protein interaction energy (Zlotnick et al., 2015; Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Zlotnick et al., 2015 and Venkatakrishnan and Zlotnick, 2016.

claim: Making the capsid surface stiffer is predicted from condensed matter theory to promote buckling transitions that lead to faceting.
source: Making the capsid surface stiffer is predicted from condensed matter theory to promote buckling transitions that lead to faceting (Lidmar et al., 2003; Klug et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lidmar et al., 2003 and Klug et al., 2006.

claim: Crosslinking Cp150 preserved capsid symmetry by allowing a compromise where CpAMs partially flattened surfaces but the stress was distributed globally.
source: We therefore suggest that crosslinking Cp150 preserved capsid symmetry by allowing a compromise where CpAMs partially flattened surfaces but the stress was distributed globally, consistent with the mechanical principles of tensegrity structures.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: Tensegrity structures can be designed to undergo structural transitions in response to relatively small stimuli.
source: Tensegrity structures can also be designed to undergo structural transitions in response to relatively small stimuli (Domitrovic et al., 2013b; Skelton et al., 2001; Fuller, 1975) in the same way that HBV responds to CpAM binding.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Domitrovic et al., 2013b, Skelton et al., 2001, and Fuller, 1975.

claim: HBV responds to CpAM binding in the same way that tensegrity structures undergo structural transitions in response to relatively small stimuli.
source: Tensegrity structures can also be designed to undergo structural transitions in response to relatively small stimuli (Domitrovic et al., 2013b; Skelton et al., 2001; Fuller, 1975) in the same way that HBV responds to CpAM binding.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn between tensegrity structures and HBV capsids.

claim: The stability of icosahedral virus capsids is fundamentally related to their symmetry.
source: Indeed, a reoccurring point in literature on the mechanical properties of icosahedral virus capsids, is that their stability is fundamentally related to their symmetry (Klug et al., 2006; Zandi et al., 2004; Zandi and Reguera, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klug et al., 2006, Zandi et al., 2004, and Zandi and Reguera, 2005.

claim: HAP-TAMRA bound capsid tightly and slowly.
source: Taking advantage of HAP-TAMRA optical properties, we observed that HAP-TAMRA bound capsid tightly and slowly.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Slow binding suggests that sites are only rarely open to CpAMs.
source: Slow binding suggests that sites are only rarely open to CpAMs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic data.

claim: The slow rate of binding is reminiscent of a proteolytic analysis of HBV capsid stability where it was observed that Cp149 capsids would undergo a slow partial unfolding transition.
source: The slow rate of binding is reminiscent of a proteolytic analysis of HBV capsid stability where it was observed that Cp149 capsids would undergo a slow partial unfolding transition (Hilmer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hilmer et al., 2008.

claim: The half-life of the unfolding transition for cleavage was on the order of 100 min.
source: The half-life of the unfolding transition for cleavage was on the order of 100 min.
evidence: This is a statement about previous experimental results.

claim: Intact capsids can persist in solution for months.
source: In contrast, intact capsids can persist in solution for months (Uetrecht et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Uetrecht et al., 2010.

claim: All-atom molecular simulations of capsids indicate that HBV capsid structure is highly dynamic and is capable of departure from icosahedral symmetry.
source: All-atom molecular simulations of capsids indicate that HBV capsid structure is highly dynamic and is capable of departure from icosahedral symmetry (Perilla et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Perilla et al., 2016.

claim: All of the bound HAP-TAMRA is involved in π-stacked dimers, even when there is on average approximately a single HAP-TAMRA per quasi-sixfold vertex.
source: The absorbance shift we observe (Figure 3f) indicates that all of the bound HAP-TAMRA is involved in π-stacked dimers, even when there is on average approximately a single HAP-TAMRA per quasi-sixfold vertex.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectroscopic data.

claim: HAP-TAMRA is not randomly distributed over a capsid.
source: This would not occur if HAP-TAMRA were randomly distributed over a capsid.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectroscopic data.

claim: In a random distribution at the lowest concentration tested only about 1/3 of the probe would be in quasi-sixfold vertices with two or more bound molecules.
source: In a random distribution at the lowest concentration we tested only about 1/3 of the probe would be in quasi-sixfold vertices with two or more bound molecules.
evidence: This is a calculation based on random distribution assumptions.

claim: The structure of the T = 4 capsid suggests interaction only between probes in the B and C' or C and B' sites.
source: Furthermore, the structure of the T = 4 capsid suggests interaction only between probes in the B and C' or C and B' sites (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: Approximately 100% of the possible signal is observed at the lowest HAP-TAMRA:dimer ratio tested.
source: Nonetheless, we observe approximately 100% of the possible signal.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: There is a high degree of cooperativity of binding, at least at a local level.
source: This indicates a high degree of cooperativity of binding, at least at a local level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spectroscopic data.

claim: Once a B site is filled there must be a preference for filing an adjacent C' with a much faster rate constant.
source: Thus, once a B site is filled there must be a preference for filing an adjacent C' with a much faster rate constant (or for a C site a preference for an adjacent B').
evidence: This is an inference based on the kinetic and spectroscopic data.

claim: Virus capsids are not inert containers.
source: In a broad sense, our results reaffirm the view that virus capsids are not inert containers.
evidence: This is a general conclusion based on the findings.

claim: Some of the most important biological functions of icosahedral capsids may occur when they become non-icosahedral.
source: It is likely that some of the most important biological functions of icosahedral capsids may occur when they become non-icosahedral.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Non-icosahedral states of HBV capsids can be induced using CpAMs.
source: We have demonstrated that non-icosahedral states of HBV capsids can be induced using CpAMs.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: A molecule which simultaneously affects two or more stages of the lifecycle would reduce the impact of escape mutations.
source: A molecule which simultaneously affects two or more stages of the lifecycle would reduce the impact of escape mutations, and increases the likelihood of clearing an infection.
evidence: This is speculation about the therapeutic implications.

claim: A molecule which simultaneously affects two or more stages of the lifecycle increases the likelihood of clearing an infection.
source: A molecule which simultaneously affects two or more stages of the lifecycle would reduce the impact of escape mutations, and increases the likelihood of clearing an infection.
evidence: This is speculation about the therapeutic implications.
